summary: Discusses the metrics to use when evaluating new or changed congestion control, including transport protocols, TCP changes, application-level control, and active queue management. It notes there is no consensus on a single goal and argues for judging trade-offs among metrics, like throughput, delay, and fairness. It is an informational document from a research group.

eli5.summary: To judge a new road traffic plan, you do not only count speed. You check waiting time and fairness too. This paper lists what to measure.

subtitle: What to measure when evaluating how networks handle traffic congestion

tldr.problem: Researchers and network engineers need a shared understanding of which metrics matter when evaluating new or modified congestion control mechanisms, but there is no consensus on whether throughput, delay, or fairness should be the priority.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5166 catalogs the key metrics that should be considered: throughput, delay, packet loss, response time to changes, fairness between flows, robustness in challenging environments, and deployability.
tldr.outcome: The document establishes that congestion control should be evaluated on trade-offs between multiple metrics rather than optimizing for a single goal, guiding research and development in the field.

facts.label: Focus
facts.value: Trade-offs between throughput, delay, and fairness

today: RFC 5166 remains a key reference for evaluating congestion control mechanisms. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and its metric framework is widely cited in network research and protocol design. The principles it outlines continue to guide work on TCP variants, QUIC, and other transport protocols.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5166 discusses the metrics used to evaluate congestion control mechanisms—the algorithms that let networks share bandwidth fairly and efficiently when many users compete for the same links. It comes from the Transport Modeling Research Group (TMRG) of the Internet Research Task Force.

The document notes there is no single agreed-upon metric. Some protocols prioritize raw throughput (sending more data), others prioritize low delay (getting data there quickly), and others focus on fairness (giving each user equal bandwidth). The RFC argues that good evaluation instead examines trade-offs: how much throughput does a mechanism gain versus how much extra delay does it introduce?
sections.eli5: Engineers argue about what makes a good traffic system. Some want cars to move fast, others want short wait times, and others want everyone to be treated fairly. This paper says you need to check all of them.

sections.title: Core Metrics for Congestion Control
sections.content:
The RFC organizes metrics into categories. Throughput measures how much data the network carries, split into aggregate bandwidth (all flows together) and per-flow rates (each user's share). Delay measures how long packets wait in queues and how long end-to-end delivery takes. Packet loss rates count dropped packets, either across the whole network or per connection.

A key trade-off appears here: a router can maximize throughput by keeping a large queue, but that increases delay. Alternatively, it can drop packets aggressively to keep delays low, but then senders retransmit and throughput suffers.

The RFC also covers response time (how quickly the network adapts when conditions change, like a sudden spike in traffic) and minimizing oscillations (preventing the sending rate from bouncing up and down wildly, which wastes bandwidth and makes packet loss synchronize across multiple connections).
sections.eli5: Speed, waiting time, and dropped messages are the big three. A network can optimize for any two of them, but not all three.

sections.title: Fairness and Convergence
sections.content:
Fairness asks: do all flows get an equal share of bandwidth? The RFC describes several fairness definitions. Jain's fairness index scores fairness on a scale from 0 (one user hogs everything) to 1 (perfect equality). Max-min fairness prioritizes helping the user with the least bandwidth first. Proportional fairness balances overall utility—it favors smaller flows but less strongly than max-min.

There is disagreement in the community about which definition is best. Fairness between flows with different path lengths or round-trip times is especially controversial: some argue a long-distance connection should not be penalized for its distance, while others say giving it the same throughput rate wastes bandwidth that could help a nearby connection.

Convergence time measures how long it takes two competing flows to reach fair sharing after one starts.
sections.eli5: If two people share a pie, fairness means they get equal slices. But what if one is hungry and the other is not? That changes how you split it. Network engineers disagree on the right answer.

sections.title: Robustness in Real-World Environments
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that congestion control must work in challenging conditions: wireless links with corruption and variable bandwidth, paths where packets arrive out of order, mobile networks that change paths suddenly, and links with asymmetric speeds.

In mobile environments, the bandwidth can change by orders of magnitude in milliseconds (a phone moving from 4G to WiFi, for example). Energy consumption also matters for mobile devices: protocols that cause excessive retransmission drain batteries faster.

The document also addresses failure modes: congestion control must detect and handle misbehaving endpoints that do not follow the protocol, and it must be robust to router failures and network misconfigurations.
sections.eli5: Roads have potholes, detours, and rush hour. A good traffic plan works when things go wrong.

sections.title: Deployability and Summary
sections.content:
Deployability considers practical obstacles to adoption. Can the mechanism be added only to the sender, or do routers need changes? Are the computational requirements simple or complex? How much does it add to packet headers?

Some proposals require changes everywhere along a path (for example, Explicit Congestion Notification at every router) or even at every middlebox like firewalls and VPNs. Others work with only sender changes (like NewReno TCP modifications), which deploy faster.

The RFC establishes that transport protocols should be benchmarked across all these metrics rather than pursuing a single goal. Researchers should ask: this protocol excels at low delay, but what does it cost in throughput or fairness? This framework enables more honest, comprehensive evaluation of new congestion control proposals.
sections.eli5: A good plan is only good if people can actually use it. Complexity and cost matter as much as performance.
